claim: Pulse wave velocity (PWV) independently predicts cardiovascular risk.
source: Pulse wave velocity (PWV) independently predicts cardiovascular risk.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hametner et al., 2013 and Vishram-Nielsen et al., 2020 in the following sentence about PWV predicting cardiovascular risk including stroke.

claim: Aortic pulse wave velocity independently predicts cardiovascular risk including stroke.
source: Aortic pulse wave velocity (PWV) which relates to vascular stiffness, independently predicts cardiovascular risk including stroke (Hametner et al., 2013; Vishram-Nielsen et al., 2020).
evidence: Directly supported by citations to Hametner et al., 2013 and Vishram-Nielsen et al., 2020.

claim: Aortic pulse wave velocity relates to vascular stiffness.
source: Aortic pulse wave velocity (PWV) which relates to vascular stiffness, independently predicts cardiovascular risk including stroke (Hametner et al., 2013; Vishram-Nielsen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the relationship between PWV and vascular stiffness, supported by the citations provided.

claim: PWV values above 10 m/s have been suggested as threshold indicating increased risk.
source: PWV values above 10 m/s have been suggested as threshold indicating increased risk (Van Bortel et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Van Bortel et al., 2012.

claim: PWV values above 10 m/s are included in current hypertension guidelines for assessing hypertension-mediated organ damage and guiding secondary prophylaxis.
source: PWV values above 10 m/s have been suggested as threshold indicating increased risk (Van Bortel et al., 2012) and are included in current hypertension guidelines for assessing hypertension-mediated organ damage and guiding secondary prophylaxis (Williams et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Williams et al., 2018.

claim: Oscillometric blood pressure monitors estimating PWV based on age and blood pressure could simplify vascular assessment.
source: Oscillometric blood pressure monitors estimating PWV based on age and blood pressure could simplify vascular assessment (Hametner et al., 2013; Hametner et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hametner et al., 2013 and Hametner et al., 2021.

claim: Estimated PWV correlates with age.
source: Indeed, estimated PWV correlates with age (Schwartz et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwartz et al., 2019.

claim: Estimated PWV correlates with invasively measured PWV.
source: Indeed, estimated PWV correlates with age (Schwartz et al., 2019) and invasively measured PWV (Hametner et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hametner et al., 2013.

claim: Oscillometric monitors for estimating PWV operate observer-independent and are easy to use.
source: These monitors operate observer-independent, are easy to use, and are, therefore, applied in clinical practice and in clinical studies alike (Paiva et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated as a characteristic of the monitors, with citation to Paiva et al., 2020 supporting their application in clinical practice and studies.

claim: Oscillometric monitors for estimating PWV are applied in clinical practice and in clinical studies.
source: These monitors operate observer-independent, are easy to use, and are, therefore, applied in clinical practice and in clinical studies alike (Paiva et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paiva et al., 2020.

claim: 163 master athletes were approached during the 23rd Masters Athletics Championships 2018 in Málaga, Spain.
source: During the 23rd Masters Athletics Championships 2018 in Málaga, Spain, we approached 163 master athletes.
evidence: Direct statement about the study methodology and participant recruitment.

claim: Athletes with atrial fibrillation or significant cardiovascular disease assessed by echocardiography were excluded.
source: We excluded athletes with atrial fibrillation or significant cardiovascular disease assessed by echocardiography.
evidence: Direct statement about exclusion criteria in the study methodology.

claim: 129 master athletes (88 men/41 women, 56 ± 11 [range 35–86] years, 24.0 ± 3.5 kg/m²) were included in the study.
source: In the remaining 129 athletes (88 men/41 women, 56 ± 11 [range 35–86] years, 24.0 ± 3.5 kg/m²), we acquired blood pressure, heart rate, and estimated PWV thrice on the same arm after 10 min supine rest (Arc-Solver-Algorithm, CardioCube, AIT, Vienna, Austria).
evidence: Direct statement of study participant characteristics and sample size.

claim: Blood pressure, heart rate, and estimated PWV were acquired thrice on the same arm after 10 min supine rest in master athletes using the Arc-Solver-Algorithm.
source: In the remaining 129 athletes (88 men/41 women, 56 ± 11 [range 35–86] years, 24.0 ± 3.5 kg/m²), we acquired blood pressure, heart rate, and estimated PWV thrice on the same arm after 10 min supine rest (Arc-Solver-Algorithm, CardioCube, AIT, Vienna, Austria).
evidence: Direct statement of measurement methodology.

claim: 24 healthy participants (16 men/8 women, 33 ± 9 years, 24.3 ± 2.1 kg/m²) participated in the AGBRESA study.
source: In 24 healthy participants (16 men/8 women, 33 ± 9 years, 24.3 ± 2.1 kg/m²) of the AGBRESA (artificial gravity bedrest) study, which was conducted in collaboration with NASA and ESA in Cologne, Germany (Hoffmann et al., 2021), we assessed estimated PWV before head-down-tilt bedrest as described above.
evidence: Direct statement of study participant characteristics and sample size.

claim: The AGBRESA study was conducted in collaboration with NASA and ESA in Cologne, Germany.
source: In 24 healthy participants (16 men/8 women, 33 ± 9 years, 24.3 ± 2.1 kg/m²) of the AGBRESA (artificial gravity bedrest) study, which was conducted in collaboration with NASA and ESA in Cologne, Germany (Hoffmann et al., 2021), we assessed estimated PWV before head-down-tilt bedrest as described above.
evidence: Direct statement about the study location and collaborators, with citation to Hoffmann et al., 2021.

claim: Estimated PWV was assessed before head-down-tilt bedrest in AGBRESA participants.
source: In 24 healthy participants (16 men/8 women, 33 ± 9 years, 24.3 ± 2.1 kg/m²) of the AGBRESA (artificial gravity bedrest) study, which was conducted in collaboration with NASA and ESA in Cologne, Germany (Hoffmann et al., 2021), we assessed estimated PWV before head-down-tilt bedrest as described above.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement timing in the study protocol.

claim: The estimated PWV has been validated against invasive catheter measurements derived from the ascending aorta to the aortic bifurcation.
source: As the estimated PWV has been validated against invasive catheter measurements derived from the ascending aorta to the aortic bifurcation (Hametner et al., 2013), we mimicked this approach non-invasively by measuring pulse wave arrival time from the electrocardiographic R-peak to the arrival of the pulse wave at an oscillometric thigh cuff.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hametner et al., 2013.

claim: Pulse wave arrival time was measured from the electrocardiographic R-peak to the arrival of the pulse wave at an oscillometric thigh cuff.
source: As the estimated PWV has been validated against invasive catheter measurements derived from the ascending aorta to the aortic bifurcation (Hametner et al., 2013), we mimicked this approach non-invasively by measuring pulse wave arrival time from the electrocardiographic R-peak to the arrival of the pulse wave at an oscillometric thigh cuff.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement methodology.

claim: Pulse wave arrival time was corrected for isovolumetric contraction time.
source: We corrected pulse wave arrival time for isovolumetric contraction time, the time from the R-peak in the ECG to aortic valve opening assessed by 2D-pulsed-wave-doppler echocardiography.
evidence: Direct statement of data processing methodology.

claim: Isovolumetric contraction time is the time from the R-peak in the ECG to aortic valve opening.
source: We corrected pulse wave arrival time for isovolumetric contraction time, the time from the R-peak in the ECG to aortic valve opening assessed by 2D-pulsed-wave-doppler echocardiography.
evidence: Direct definition provided in the text.

claim: Isovolumetric contraction time was assessed by 2D-pulsed-wave-doppler echocardiography.
source: We corrected pulse wave arrival time for isovolumetric contraction time, the time from the R-peak in the ECG to aortic valve opening assessed by 2D-pulsed-wave-doppler echocardiography.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement methodology.

claim: Corrected pulse wave arrival time represents pulse wave travel time from the aortic valve opening to the arrival at the thigh.
source: Corrected pulse wave arrival time represents pulse wave travel time from the aortic valve opening to the arrival at the thigh.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the meaning of the corrected measurement.

claim: The jugulum-thigh cuff measurement approach includes the ascending aorta and the aortic arc.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the carotid-femoral PWV, this approach includes the ascending aorta and the aortic arc, which are commonly affected by aging-associated vascular disease.
evidence: Direct statement about what anatomical structures are included in the measurement approach.

claim: The ascending aorta and the aortic arc are commonly affected by aging-associated vascular disease.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the carotid-femoral PWV, this approach includes the ascending aorta and the aortic arc, which are commonly affected by aging-associated vascular disease.
evidence: Statement based on established medical knowledge about vascular aging.

claim: Measured PWV was calculated by dividing jugulum-thigh cuff distance by corrected pulse wave arrival time.
source: Dividing jugulum-thigh cuff distance by corrected pulse wave arrival time resulted in measured PWV.
evidence: Direct statement of calculation methodology.

claim: All subjects provided informed consent and consent to publish before enrollment.
source: All subjects provided informed consent and consent to publish before enrollment.
evidence: Direct statement about ethical procedures.

claim: The bedrest study was approved by the Northrine-Medical-Association ethics committee (2018143).
source: The bedrest study as well as the study in master athletes was approved by the Northrine-Medical-Association (Ärztekammer Nordrhein, 2018143 and 2018171) ethics committee and registered at the German Clinical Trial Register (DRKS00015677 and DRKS00015172).
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: The study in master athletes was approved by the Northrine-Medical-Association ethics committee (2018171).
source: The bedrest study as well as the study in master athletes was approved by the Northrine-Medical-Association (Ärztekammer Nordrhein, 2018143 and 2018171) ethics committee and registered at the German Clinical Trial Register (DRKS00015677 and DRKS00015172).
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: The bedrest study was registered at the German Clinical Trial Register (DRKS00015677).
source: The bedrest study as well as the study in master athletes was approved by the Northrine-Medical-Association (Ärztekammer Nordrhein, 2018143 and 2018171) ethics committee and registered at the German Clinical Trial Register (DRKS00015677 and DRKS00015172).
evidence: Direct statement about trial registration.

claim: The study in master athletes was registered at the German Clinical Trial Register (DRKS00015172).
source: The bedrest study as well as the study in master athletes was approved by the Northrine-Medical-Association (Ärztekammer Nordrhein, 2018143 and 2018171) ethics committee and registered at the German Clinical Trial Register (DRKS00015677 and DRKS00015172).
evidence: Direct statement about trial registration.

claim: All data were normally distributed according to Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
source: According to Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, all data were normally distributed, and results are reported as mean values ± standard deviation.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical testing of data distribution.

claim: Results are reported as mean values ± standard deviation.
source: According to Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, all data were normally distributed, and results are reported as mean values ± standard deviation.
evidence: Direct statement about data reporting format.

claim: A quadratic regression model was used based on other cardiovascular risk estimate models.
source: Based on other cardiovascular risk estimate models, we used a quadratic regression model.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical methodology choice based on precedent from other models.

claim: Resting heart rate was 61 ± 11 bpm in master athletes.
source: Resting heart rate was 61 ± 11 bpm, and blood pressure was 128 ± 15/78 ± 8 mmHg in master athletes.
evidence: Direct statement of measured data.

claim: Blood pressure was 128 ± 15/78 ± 8 mmHg in master athletes.
source: Resting heart rate was 61 ± 11 bpm, and blood pressure was 128 ± 15/78 ± 8 mmHg in master athletes.
evidence: Direct statement of measured data.

claim: Estimated PWV ranged from 5.5 to 14.5 with a mean of 8.3 ± 1.8 m/s in master athletes.
source: Estimated PWV ranged from 5.5 to 14.5 with a mean of 8.3 ± 1.8 m/s.
evidence: Direct statement of measured data.

claim: In a quadratic regression model, age and mean arterial pressure predicted estimated PWV (beta value 0.93 and 0.14, p<0.001) in master athletes.
source: In a quadratic regression model, age and mean arterial pressure predicted estimated PWV (beta value 0.93 and 0.14, p<0.001), whereas, sex and BMI had no influence.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: Sex and BMI had no influence on estimated PWV in master athletes.
source: In a quadratic regression model, age and mean arterial pressure predicted estimated PWV (beta value 0.93 and 0.14, p<0.001), whereas, sex and BMI had no influence.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: The quadratic regression model explained 95% (R² = 0.95) of estimated PWV's variance in master athletes.
source: The model explained 95% (R² = 0.95) of estimated PWV's variance.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: Age alone explained 90% (R² = 0.90) of estimated PWV's variance in master athletes.
source: Age alone explained 90% (R² = 0.90).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: Resting heart rate was 62 ± 9 bpm in the AGBRESA bedrest study.
source: Resting heart rate was 62 ± 9 bpm, and blood pressure was 125 ± 11/70 ± 7 mmHg in the AGBRESA bedrest study.
evidence: Direct statement of measured data.

claim: Blood pressure was 125 ± 11/70 ± 7 mmHg in the AGBRESA bedrest study.
source: Resting heart rate was 62 ± 9 bpm, and blood pressure was 125 ± 11/70 ± 7 mmHg in the AGBRESA bedrest study.
evidence: Direct statement of measured data.

claim: Estimated PWV was 5.8 ± 1.1 m/s in the AGBRESA bedrest study.
source: Estimated PWV was 5.8 ± 1.1 m/s, and measured PWV was 4.8 ± 0.6.
evidence: Direct statement of measured data.

claim: Measured PWV was 4.8 ± 0.6 m/s in the AGBRESA bedrest study.
source: Estimated PWV was 5.8 ± 1.1 m/s, and measured PWV was 4.8 ± 0.6.
evidence: Direct statement of measured data.

claim: Age and estimated PWV were highly correlated (R² 0.88, p<0.001) in the AGBRESA study.
source: Age and estimated PWV were highly correlated (R² 0.88, p<0.001, Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The correlation between measured PWV and age was weaker (R² 0.55, p<0.001) than the correlation between estimated PWV and age.
source: The correlation between measured PWV and age was weaker (R² 0.55, p<0.001).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results with implicit comparison to the previously stated R² of 0.88 for estimated PWV.

claim: In a quadratic regression model, age (beta value 0.99, p<0.001) predicted estimated PWV in the AGBRESA study.
source: In a quadratic regression model, age (beta value 0.99, p<0.001) but not BMI, sex, or mean arterial pressure predicted estimated PWV.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: BMI, sex, and mean arterial pressure did not predict estimated PWV in the AGBRESA study.
source: In a quadratic regression model, age (beta value 0.99, p<0.001) but not BMI, sex, or mean arterial pressure predicted estimated PWV.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: The quadratic regression model explained 98% of estimated PWV's variance in the AGBRESA study.
source: The model explained 98% of estimated PWV's variance.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: R² between estimated and measured PWV was 0.40 (p<0.05) in the AGBRESA study.
source: R² between estimated and measured PWV was 0.40 (p<0.05).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: An increasing bias between estimated and measured PWV with advancing age was observed.
source: We observed an increasing bias between estimated and measured PWV with advancing age with an average 0.96 ± 0.83 m/s difference between methods (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement of observed pattern with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The mean difference between estimated and measured PWV was 0.96 ± 0.83 m/s.
source: We observed an increasing bias between estimated and measured PWV with advancing age with an average 0.96 ± 0.83 m/s difference between methods (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement of measured data with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: When adjusting the correlation of measured and estimated PWV for age, no significant relationship was observed (p=0.267).
source: When adjusting the correlation of measured and estimated PWV for age we could no longer observe a significant relationship (p=0.267).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: Measurements were repeated in one male person in his 50s with normal BMI with randomly changed entered age.
source: To assess influences of entered rather than chronological age on estimated PWV, we repeated measurements in one male person, who is in his 50s and has normal BMI, and randomly changed the entered age in decades from 30 to 80 years.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methodology.

claim: Measurements were obtained thrice at each entered age decade from 30 to 80 years in the single subject experiment.
source: We obtained measurements in each entered age decade thrice.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methodology.

claim: Estimated PWV related to entered age (R² 0.996, p<0.001) in the single subject experiment.
source: Again, estimated PWV related to entered age (R² 0.996, p<0.001, Figure 1C) akin to the relationship between estimated PWV and chronological age in athletes and in bedrest study participants.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The relationship between estimated PWV and entered age in the single subject was similar to the relationship between estimated PWV and chronological age in athletes and bedrest study participants.
source: Again, estimated PWV related to entered age (R² 0.996, p<0.001, Figure 1C) akin to the relationship between estimated PWV and chronological age in athletes and in bedrest study participants.
evidence: Direct comparison statement based on the data analysis.

claim: An almost perfect correlation between estimated PWV and age was observed in two independent cohorts.
source: Similarly to other studies (Schwartz et al., 2019), we observed an almost perfect correlation between estimated PWV and age in two independent cohorts.
evidence: Direct statement of findings with citation to Schwartz et al., 2019 for comparison.

claim: Estimated PWV in elite Master Athletes and in healthy bedrest study participants of average physical fitness were located on the same regression line.
source: Strikingly, estimated PWV in elite Master Athletes, which would be expected to benefit from lifelong exercise, and in healthy bedrest study participants of average physical fitness were located on the same regression line.
evidence: Direct statement of observed pattern in the data.

claim: Elite Master Athletes would be expected to benefit from lifelong exercise.
source: Strikingly, estimated PWV in elite Master Athletes, which would be expected to benefit from lifelong exercise, and in healthy bedrest study participants of average physical fitness were located on the same regression line.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about exercise benefits.

claim: A previous study showed significantly lower measured PWV in endurance trained compared with sedentary older men.
source: A previous study showed significantly lower measured PWV in endurance trained compared with sedentary older men (Vaitkevicius et al., 1993) making a methodological limitation more likely.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vaitkevicius et al., 1993.

claim: The finding that endurance trained older men have lower measured PWV makes a methodological limitation of estimated PWV more likely.
source: A previous study showed significantly lower measured PWV in endurance trained compared with sedentary older men (Vaitkevicius et al., 1993) making a methodological limitation more likely.
evidence: Inference drawn from the cited study to explain the current findings.

claim: Estimated PWV substantially overestimated PWV, particularly in older persons.
source: Indeed, in our study, estimated PWV substantially overestimated PWV, particularly in older persons.
evidence: Direct statement of findings from the study data.

claim: The modest correlation between estimated and measured PWV was attenuated after adjusting for age.
source: Moreover, the modest correlation between estimated and measured PWV was attenuated after adjusting for age in our relatively small bedrest cohort.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: In a previous study, estimated PWV highly correlated with PWV calculated solely from age and blood pressure.
source: Finally, in a previous study, estimated PWV highly correlated with PWV calculated solely from age and blood pressure (Hametner et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hametner et al., 2021.

claim: The algorithm providing PWV estimates appears to weigh age so strongly that subtle influences on vascular wall properties caused by hemodynamic changes and physical training cannot be discerned.
source: Thus, the algorithm providing PWV estimates appears to weigh age so strongly that subtle influences on vascular wall properties caused by hemodynamic changes and physical training cannot be discerned.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study findings and previous literature.

claim: Estimated PWV mainly reflects data entered prior to measuring blood pressure rather than true vascular properties.
source: Even more so, estimated PWV mainly reflects data entered prior to measuring blood pressure rather than true vascular properties.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study findings, particularly the single-subject experiment.

claim: Estimated PWV is no substitute for measured PWV.
source: The clinical implication is that estimated PWV is no substitute for measured PWV, which likely limits the utility of the methodology in individualizing risk assessment.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: The utility of estimated PWV methodology is limited in individualizing risk assessment.
source: The clinical implication is that estimated PWV is no substitute for measured PWV, which likely limits the utility of the methodology in individualizing risk assessment.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: Simply asking the patient for age and measuring blood pressure provides almost as much information as estimating PWV.
source: In fact, simply asking the patient in front of us for his or her age and measuring blood pressure provides almost as much information as estimating PWV.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study findings showing the dominant influence of age on estimated PWV.

claim: Vascular aging assessment using established methodologies rather than estimates should be considered.
source: Instead, vascular aging assessment using established methodologies rather than estimates should be considered (Jordan et al., 2015).
evidence: Recommendation based on study findings, with citation to Jordan et al., 2015.

claim: Estimated PWV very highly correlated with age (R2 = 0.90) in master athletes.
source: Estimated pulse velocity very highly correlated with age (R2 = 0.90) in master athletes.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results from the abstract.

claim: Estimated PWV values in master athletes were located on the same regression line as values obtained in participants of the head down tilt bed rest study.
source: Estimated PWV values were located on the same regression line like values obtained in participants of the head down tilt bed rest study.
evidence: Direct statement of findings from the abstract.

claim: The correlation between estimated and measured PWV was modest (R² 0.40; p<0.05).
source: The modest correlation between estimated and measured PWV (R² 0.40; p<0.05) was attenuated after adjusting for age
evidence: Direct statement of statistical analysis results from the abstract.

claim: The mean difference between estimated and measured PWV was 1 m/s.
source: the mean difference between PWV measurements was 1 m/s.
evidence: Direct statement of measured data from the abstract.

claim: Estimated PWV failed to detect beneficial effects of lifelong exercise.
source: Estimated PWV mainly reflects the entered age rather than true vascular properties and, therefore, failed detecting beneficial effects of lifelong exercise.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study findings stated in the abstract.
